\section[l'alerte]{l'alerte — the alert, the alarm}

\label{lesson:FR-C301-alerte}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the French for the tourniquet, then the French for the stretcher.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: l'alerte}
\textbf{l'alerte} — \textquotedblleft{}the alert, the alarm\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
L'alerte a été donnée à trois heures du matin.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The alarm was raised at three in the morning.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Donner l'alerte} — to raise the alarm; \emph{une alerte à la bombe} — a bomb scare.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{alerte} is usually traced to Italian \emph{all'erta} \textquotedblleft{}on the lookout, on the height\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB lists the French word without a parent).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{l'alerte}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{l'alerte}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{l'alerte}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the French for the tourniquet, then the French for the stretcher, then say \emph{l'alerte} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does l'alerte mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The alert, the alarm\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[alerter]{alerter — to alert, to warn}

\label{lesson:FR-C301-alerter}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the French for the stretcher, then the French for the alert.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: alerter}
\textbf{alerter} — \textquotedblleft{}to alert, to warn\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Un voisin a alerté les pompiers.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{A neighbour alerted the fire brigade.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Alerter la police} — to call the police.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{alerter} is built on \emph{alerte} \textquotedblleft{}alert\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), which is usually traced to Italian \emph{all'erta} \textquotedblleft{}on the lookout\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[le défibrillateur]{le défibrillateur — the defibrillator}

\label{lesson:FR-C301-defibrillateur}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the French for the alert, then the French for to alert.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: le défibrillateur}
\textbf{le défibrillateur} — \textquotedblleft{}the defibrillator\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Il y a un défibrillateur à l'entrée de la mairie.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{There is a defibrillator at the entrance of the town hall.}
\end{quote}

Often in public places, in a box on the wall.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{défibrillateur} is a learned medical word built on \emph{fibrillation}, from Latin \emph{fibrilla} \textquotedblleft{}a small fibre\textquotedblright{}, from \emph{fibra} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{le défibrillateur}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{le défibrillateur}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{le défibrillateur}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the French for the alert, then the French for to alert, then say \emph{le défibrillateur} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[la sortie de secours]{la sortie de secours — the emergency exit}

\label{lesson:FR-C301-sortie-de-secours}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the French for to alert, then the French for the defibrillator.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la sortie de secours}
\textbf{la sortie de secours} — \textquotedblleft{}the emergency exit\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Les gens sont sortis par la sortie de secours.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{People went out through the emergency exit.}
\end{quote}

Signs also say \emph{issue de secours}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{sortie} is built on \emph{sortir} \textquotedblleft{}to go out\textquotedblright{}, which is usually traced to Latin \emph{sortīrī} \textquotedblleft{}to draw lots\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short; EtymDB lists no parent); \emph{secours} is inherited from Latin \emph{succursus} \textquotedblleft{}help\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la sortie de secours}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la sortie de secours}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{la sortie de secours}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the French for to alert, then the French for the defibrillator, then say \emph{la sortie de secours} again
\end{itemize}

\section[évacuer]{évacuer — to evacuate, to clear}

\label{lesson:FR-C301-evacuer}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the French for the defibrillator, then the French for the emergency exit.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: évacuer}
\textbf{évacuer} — \textquotedblleft{}to evacuate, to clear\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
La police a évacué le bâtiment.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The police evacuated the building.}
\end{quote}

Also of water: \emph{évacuer l'eau de pluie} — to drain away rainwater.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{évacuer} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{ēvacuāre} \textquotedblleft{}to empty out\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), built on \emph{vacuus} \textquotedblleft{}empty\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the French for the defibrillator, then the French for the emergency exit, then say \emph{évacuer} again
